questions.q: What communication problem does Lightning Message Service solve that custom events (Lessons 9-11) cannot?
options: Passing a payload larger than a few kilobytes between components
Allowing a component to call Apex without the @wire decorator
Letting two components with no parent-child relationship -- including LWC, Aura, and Visualforce -- communicate without chaining events through every intermediate layer
Making a component's CSS styles apply to a sibling component
questions.explain: LMS exists specifically for components that aren't related in the component tree at all -- it removes the need to chain custom events through every intermediate layer, and it also works across LWC, Aura, and Visualforce.

questions.q: What does a `.messageChannel-meta.xml` file actually define?
options: A component's public API surface
The list of Apex classes a component is allowed to call
The CSS styling shared across a design system
A named, shared channel that components can publish messages to and subscribe to receive messages from, independent of any component hierarchy
questions.explain: A Lightning Message Channel is its own metadata type defining a named channel, with optional declared fields, that any component on the page can publish to or subscribe from.

questions.q: Why does wiring `MessageContext` (rather than calling `createMessageContext()` manually) simplify a component that only needs to publish or subscribe while it's on the page?
options: Wiring MessageContext is required -- createMessageContext() no longer exists
Wiring MessageContext makes the component's subscription bubble up through the DOM
The wire service manages the message context's lifecycle automatically, so the component doesn't have to manually call releaseMessageContext() itself
Wiring MessageContext allows publishing without specifying a channel
questions.explain: Wiring MessageContext hands lifecycle management to the wire service automatically. A component that instead calls createMessageContext() directly is responsible for calling releaseMessageContext() itself in disconnectedCallback().

questions.q: In the subscriber example, why does `subscribe()` happen in `connectedCallback()` and `unsubscribe()` happen in `disconnectedCallback()`?
options: Pairing subscribe/unsubscribe with connectedCallback/disconnectedCallback guarantees the subscription's lifetime matches the component's own lifetime, avoiding a subscription that outlives the component
Those are simply the only two hooks that exist in LWC
connectedCallback is the only hook where publish() is allowed to run
disconnectedCallback runs before connectedCallback, so the order doesn't actually matter
questions.explain: Subscribing when the component connects and unsubscribing when it disconnects ties the subscription's lifetime to the component's own -- without that pairing, a stale subscription could keep handling messages after the component is gone.

questions.q: What happens if a component's message-channel subscription is never released?
options: The Salesforce org automatically releases it after 24 hours
The channel itself becomes permanently unusable by any other component
Nothing -- unreleased subscriptions have no negative effect
It keeps listening even after the component that created it is gone, which can cause duplicate handling of messages or memory that never gets released
questions.explain: An unreleased subscription continues listening past the lifetime of the component that created it, which risks duplicate message handling and unreleased memory -- this is exactly why cleanup in disconnectedCallback() matters.
